title: Orbital Angular Momentum Transfer and Beam-Quality Limits in Fork-Grating Electron Diffraction
authors: P. K. Tsiopa, S. S. Baturin
abstract: We analyze fork-grating generation of electron vortex beams beyond the ideal single-mode approximation. The incident beam is described as a paraxial Gaussian ensemble with finite transverse momentum spread and a first electromagnetic Hartree phase accumulated before the grating. Within Fresnel propagation we derive an analytical expression for each diffraction order and determine the corresponding orbital-angular-momentum statistics. The mean OAM of a selected order remains fixed by the topological rule, $\langle L_z\rangle_m=mp\hbar$, while its variance is set by the residual transverse momentum spread of the beam prepared at the grating. For the Gaussian mixture, the transverse purity is $\mathcal P_{\perp,m}=[1+2(ΔL_{z,m}/\hbar)^2]^{-1}$. The observed annular profile is governed by a separate propagation-dependent blurring scale, so a beam can retain well-defined mean OAM while having low transverse purity or a partially filled vortex minimum. Within the radial phase-screen approximation, the Hartree self-field modifies the propagated profile while preserving the full-plane OAM moments and transverse purity.
summary: This work theoretically investigates how electron beams generate and propagate vortex beams using a fork-grating, accounting for non-ideal beam properties and space-charge effects. It establishes that while the mean OAM is topologically protected, the beam's transverse purity is limited by the variance of the OAM. The analysis uses advanced wave propagation techniques under several key approximations.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the transfer of Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) and the resulting beam-quality limits when generating electron vortex beams using a fork-grating structure.
main_result: The mean OAM ($\langle L_z angle_m$) is robustly fixed by the topological rule ($\langle L_z angle_m = m\hbar$), while the transverse purity ($P_{\perp,m}$) is determined by the variance of the OAM ($\Delta L_{z,m}$).
method: The analysis uses Fresnel propagation and the quasistatic electromagnetic Hartree approximation to derive analytical expressions for diffraction orders and OAM statistics.
model_or_system: The system involves an electron beam modeled as a paraxial Gaussian ensemble passing through a fork-grating, preceded by an interaction with a space-charge potential (Hartree self-field).
key_observables: Mean OAM ($\langle L_z angle_m$), Transverse Purity ($P_{\perp,m}$), OAM Dispersion ($\Delta L_{z,m}$), and the final diffracted beam profile.

main_assumptions: The derivation relies on several smallness conditions, including the paraxial approximation and the first-Hartree eikonal phase screen, which neglects higher-order self-field effects.
paper_structure: The paper builds from modeling the incident beam and the effect of the Hartree potential, through deriving the diffraction orders using Fresnel propagation, and finally calculating the OAM statistics and beam purity.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding how fundamental quantum numbers like OAM are preserved or degraded in complex wave propagation scenarios involving strong electromagnetic interactions, relevant to quantum beam shaping.

FIG. 2. Displacement of single-component diffraction profiles for m = 1 due to residual transverse tilt. The blue and red curves correspond to kx = 0 and kx = 107 m−1, respectively, with ky = 0, at z −ζ = 3 mm in the low-density regime described in the text. The profiles of Eq. (33) are shown along the positive x axis of the compensated selected order; the plotting labels (ρ0, θ0) denote the common coordinates (ρ, θ). The tilted component is displaced by αm = (z −ζ)kx/k [Eq. (26)], and its vortex zero remains at its own displaced center.

FIG. 3. Effect of incoherent transverse-momentum averaging on the observed diffraction profile for m = 1 at z −ζ = 3 mm, with negligible Hartree correction. The blue curve is the centered component kx = ky = 0; the red curve is the ensemble profile of Eq. (34) for the Gaussian distribution in Eq. (19), with σk = 107 m−1. Both curves are line profiles along the positive x axis, with ρ0 = ρ and θ0 = θ = 0. Averaging over the displaced component centers fills the intensity minimum at the mean beam center and smooths the radial oscillations.

FIG. 4. Diffraction profiles including the common radial electromagnetic Hartree phase for m = 1 of Eq. (17), at z−ζ = 3 mm. The blue curve represents the centered component kx = ky = 0; the red curve represents the incoherent Gaussian ensemble with σk = 107 m−1. The curves are plotted along the positive x axis, using ρ0 = ρ and θ0 = θ = 0. The broader radial structure compared with Fig. 3 illustrates the defocusing action of the Hartree phase. The scale ρc in Eq. (35) characterizes the exponential branch of the solution. This common radial phase preserves the full-plane OAM moments and transverse-state purity. The concentration for this figure is taken as n = 1018m−3 and ˜χem ≈1.5 × 1014.
